t: LeetCode 1540 — Can Convert String in K Moves
o: Move number i shifts one untouched index forward by EXACTLY i letters (wrapping z to a). Converting s[i] into t[i] therefore consumes a distance d = (t[i] - s[i]) mod 26, realized by any move numbered d, d + 26, d + 52, ... Multiple positions demanding the same distance must use successive elements of that progression. Example 2 fails because "abc" -> "bcd" has three demands of d = 1 needing moves 1, 27 and 53 while k = 10; example 3 succeeds because two demands of d = 1 fit into moves 1 and 27 when k = 27. So feasibility reduces to checking the largest move required by each distance class against k.
k: Per position only (t[i] - s[i]) mod 26 matters; identical distances compete for the same arithmetic progression d, d+26, d+52, ....
If distance d occurs cnt times, the last occurrence needs move d + 26*(cnt-1); the conversion fits iff that value is <= k for every d.
Unequal lengths make conversion impossible regardless of k.

a.n: Approach 1: Tally Distances, Check Worst Move
a.i: Count how many positions require each shift distance d in 1..25. Their greedy assignment uses moves d, d+26, ..., so the largest consumed move is d + 26*(cnt[d]-1). Feasibility is simply that this stays within k for all d — one counting pass plus 25 checks.
s: Tally need[(t[i] - s[i]) mod 26] over all positions.
For each d from 1 to 25 compute lastMove = d + 26 * (need[d] - 1).
Return false if any lastMove exceeds k, otherwise true.
a.t: O(n + 26) — a single counting pass plus constant-time verification.

a.n: Approach 2: Streaming Demand Tracking with Early Exit
a.i: The same math run online: process pairs one at a time, handing each demand d the next unused element d + 26*used[d] of its progression. The moment an assigned move overshoots k we can answer false without reading further, which pays off on adversarial early failures.
s: Iterate over position pairs computing d = diff mod 26.
Skip d = 0 since those characters already match.
Compute move = d + 26 * used[d]; return false if move > k.
a.t: O(n) — one streaming pass, possibly earlier.

w: Narrate the progression-per-distance argument — it proves the greedy smallest-move assignment is optimal. Pitfalls: forgetting the +26 before mod when the raw difference is negative, misreading move i as granting UP TO i shifts rather than exactly i, and overflowing 32-bit ints via 26*count in Java/C++. Edge cases: s equals t (true even for k = 0), k = 0 with any real demand, heavy skew such as many a->b pairs. Likely follow-ups: report the minimum feasible k (max of d + 26*(cnt-1)), or extend the alphabet beyond 26 letters.
